claims.text: Cold spray deposition of a hard, corrosion-resistant composite coating can repair localized surface damage on high-value components susceptible to hot cracking during fusion welding.
Cold spray forms a dense coating layer.
Cold spray forms a well-adhered coating layer.
Cold spray produces a refined or finely grained coating microstructure.
The coating is mechanically bonded to the substrate.
Cold spray creates a minimal heat-affected zone.
The dense coating acts as a barrier against crack initiation and propagation.
High-velocity particle kinetic energy consolidates the coating without significant heat input.
Cold spray minimizes residual stresses relative to a high-thermal-input repair.
Cold spray minimizes thermal distortion relative to a high-thermal-input repair.
Reduced heat input, residual stress, and thermal distortion prevent hot cracking.
The cold-sprayed surface will delay surface-defect initiation relative to fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed surface will have greater hardness than fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed surface will have a lower wear rate than fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed surface will have greater corrosion resistance than fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The process can maintain the substrate temperature well below melting and thereby limit thermal impact.
The coating is intended to retain its benefits during mechanical wear, chemical corrosion, and thermal cycling.
The intervention is expected to be most effective for localized damage where adequate coating adhesion can be achieved.
Performance under extreme mechanical loads, unusually severe chemical exposure, or extensive surface damage is unvalidated.
Long-term coating adhesion and performance under highly variable service conditions remain uncertain.
